content: 1. Excess human mortality is a critical concern in the context of helminth infections, necessitating a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying host immune responses to these parasites. This knowledge must be translated into rational strategies for vaccine development to mitigate the burden of these infections. 2. Comprehensive annotation of parasite genomes and transcriptomes is essential. This includes the development of advanced tools for functional genomics in key helminth species, enabling targeted research and intervention strategies. 3. It is imperative to define the genetic and ecological structures of parasite populations, as well as their vectors and intermediate hosts. This should be done in the context of genetic responses to interventions, parasite transmission dynamics, and epidemiological patterns, both within and between populations. 4. Research must focus on optimizing the deployment of existing intervention tools, such as pharmaceuticals, vaccines, vector control measures, and ecohealth approaches (e.g., sanitation, clean water, improved nutrition, and education). Sustainability of these interventions depends on minimizing drug resistance and maintaining community support. 5. Novel control tools must be developed to enhance the impact and sustainability of interventions. These tools should include innovative pharmaceuticals, vaccines, vector control strategies, and ecohealth approaches, with an emphasis on optimal and cost-effective delivery mechanisms. 6. Diagnostic tests need significant improvement in terms of sensitivity, specificity, multiplex capacity, and the ability to measure infection intensity and detect drug resistance. Enhanced diagnostics are particularly crucial for identifying low-prevalence infections in elimination settings and confirming the absence of infection post-treatment. 7. Standardized and validated methodologies, along with cost-effective protocols, are required for diagnosis in monitoring and evaluation (M&E) settings. This ensures consistent and reliable data collection for program assessment. 8. Strategies must be developed to integrate multiple interventions at various levels to maximize the sustainability of control programs. This is especially important for integrated neglected tropical disease (NTD) control efforts. 9. Research should address gender-specific issues to increase awareness of health processes, community participation, ownership, empowerment, and equitable access to health services for at-risk groups and communities. 10. Advanced models are needed to investigate the relationships between infection and associated morbidities. These models should account for the cumulative effects of chronic disease to evaluate disease burden and the impact of control interventions effectively. 11. Epidemiological models must be utilized more extensively to support M&E, surveillance, and the design of cost-effective sampling protocols. These models should also monitor intervention efficacy, including drug resistance, and be linked to cost-effectiveness analyses of interventions and their alternatives. 12. Investigating how helminth parasites modulate host-parasite interactions at both population and within-host levels is critical. This includes studying the effects of concurrent infections with other pathogens, the impact of parasite control interventions on these interactions, and how co-infections influence clinical outcomes and vaccine seroconversion. 13. Efforts to annotate parasite genomes and transcriptomes must continue, alongside the development of new tools for functional genomics research in key helminth species. This will provide deeper insights into parasite biology and potential therapeutic targets.
